category: Plurals made by changing the vowel

entries.meaning: An adult male human — and, in older or more formal usage, a human being of any sex. Every compound ending in -man pluralizes the same way, and in all of them the syllable is reduced to /-mən/ in the singular and /-mɛn/ or, in fast speech, also /-mən/ in the plural.
examples: A man in a gray coat asked for directions.
Three men were waiting by the gate.
She trusts that man completely.
Man has always looked at the stars and wondered.
It is the oldest tool man ever made.
Two firemen carried the ladder between them.
The chairmen of both committees signed the letter.
Both salespeople met their quota. (neutral form, regular plural)
Hey, man, can you move your car?
Oh man, I completely forgot.

senses.head: An adult male human
body: The core, everyday sense. (мужчина)
examples: A man in a gray coat asked for directions.
Three men were waiting by the gate.
She trusts that man completely.

senses.head: A human being; people in general
body: Older and now marked. Man without an article, meaning humanity, survives in fixed phrases and formal writing, but modern American usage prefers humans, people, or humankind — early humans, not early man, in current science writing. (человек; человечество)
examples: Man has always looked at the stars and wondered.
It is the oldest tool man ever made.

senses.head: In compounds
body: -man compounds inherit the irregular plural whole: policeman → policemen, fireman → firemen, salesman → salesmen. Note that many are now routinely replaced by neutral forms in American English — police officer, firefighter, salesperson — and those take a regular -s. (в составе сложных слов)
examples: Two firemen carried the ladder between them.
The chairmen of both committees signed the letter.
Both salespeople met their quota. (neutral form, regular plural)

senses.head: As a form of address, and as an interjection
body: Informal and very common in American speech, addressed to anyone regardless of sex. (чувак; ну ты даёшь)
examples: Hey, man, can you move your car?
Oh man, I completely forgot.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the men are waiting
entries.contrast: ✗ mans is never a noun plural. Man's with an apostrophe is the possessive (one man's opinion), and mans exists only as a verb (he mans the desk on Fridays).

entries.meaning: An adult female human. The most mispronounced plural in the language for learners, because the spelling and the sound change in different places.
examples: A woman at the next table recognized him.
Four women founded the company.
The women in my family all live past ninety.
Women were admitted to the college in 1972.
The magazine is written for women over forty.
Both congresswomen voted against the bill.
The saleswomen worked on commission.

senses.head: An adult female human
body: The core, everyday sense. (женщина)
examples: A woman at the next table recognized him.
Four women founded the company.
The women in my family all live past ninety.

senses.head: Women collectively, as a group in society
body: Usually plural and without an article. (женщины)
examples: Women were admitted to the college in 1972.
The magazine is written for women over forty.

senses.head: In compounds
body: Same behavior as -man: businesswoman → businesswomen, spokeswoman → spokeswomen. (в составе сложных слов)
examples: Both congresswomen voted against the bill.
The saleswomen worked on commission.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the women are waiting
entries.pattern: vowel change /ʊ/ → /ɪ/ in the first syllable
entries.contrast: The trap is the sound, not the spelling. The written change is -a- → -e- in the second syllable, but the change you actually hear is /ʊ/ → /ɪ/ in the first: WUUM-uhn → WIM-in. Say the plural wrong and it sounds like the singular.

entries.meaning: The body part below the ankle; also a unit of length equal to twelve inches, and by extension the bottom of anything upright.
examples: He broke his foot playing basketball.
My feet are killing me after that walk.
She stood barefoot, both feet in the cold sand.
The ceiling is nine feet high.
He's six foot two. (conversational; also six feet two)
They built a ten-foot wall around the property.
The cabin sits at the foot of the mountain.
A note at the foot of the page explains the symbol.
She left her slippers at the foot of the bed.
I think I got off on the wrong foot with her.
He put his foot in his mouth again at dinner.
We'll have to go on foot from here.

senses.head: The body part
body: (ступня, нога)
examples: He broke his foot playing basketball.
My feet are killing me after that walk.
She stood barefoot, both feet in the cold sand.

senses.head: A unit of length — twelve inches
body: In this sense American speech often keeps foot even where a plural is expected, especially with a following inches figure: five foot ten. As a modifier before a noun it is always singular. (фут)
examples: The ceiling is nine feet high.
He's six foot two. (conversational; also six feet two)
They built a ten-foot wall around the property.

senses.head: The bottom or base of something
body: Of a hill, a bed, a page, a staircase. (подножие, низ)
examples: The cabin sits at the foot of the mountain.
A note at the foot of the page explains the symbol.
She left her slippers at the foot of the bed.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
body: These do not vary — learn them whole. (в устойчивых выражениях)
examples: I think I got off on the wrong foot with her.
He put his foot in his mouth again at dinner.
We'll have to go on foot from here.

entries.contrast: Foots is not a plural. But note the fixed measurement phrase: before a noun, Americans say a six-foot fence, singular — the hyphenated modifier never takes the plural.

entries.meaning: One of the hard structures in the mouth; also, by extension, any of the projecting points on a comb, a saw, or a gear.
examples: The dentist pulled one tooth and filled two others.
Brush your teeth before bed.
She knocked out a front tooth in the fall.
Two teeth were missing from the comb.
The gear's teeth had worn smooth after years of use.
He was fighting tooth and nail to keep the house.
The new law has no teeth — nobody enforces it.
I'm lying through my teeth and she knows it.

senses.head: The body part
body: (зуб)
examples: The dentist pulled one tooth and filled two others.
Brush your teeth before bed.
She knocked out a front tooth in the fall.

senses.head: A projecting point on a tool or machine
body: (зубец, зуб)
examples: Two teeth were missing from the comb.
The gear's teeth had worn smooth after years of use.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
body: (в устойчивых выражениях)
examples: He was fighting tooth and nail to keep the house.
The new law has no teeth — nobody enforces it.
I'm lying through my teeth and she knows it.

entries.agreement: plural verb — her teeth are straight
entries.contrast: ✗ tooths does not exist. The adjective is toothed, and the verb teethe /tiːð/ — with a voiced th — means to grow one's first teeth.

entries.meaning: A large water bird; also, informally, a foolish person.
examples: A goose nested by the pond every spring.
Canada geese covered the entire soccer field.
We roasted a goose for the holiday.
Don't be such a goose — of course they invited you.
Her skin broke out in goose bumps. (also goosebumps; the modifier stays singular)
That was a wild goose chase — the address didn't even exist.
What's good for the goose is good for the gander.

senses.head: The bird
body: (гусь)
examples: A goose nested by the pond every spring.
Canada geese covered the entire soccer field.
We roasted a goose for the holiday.

senses.head: A silly person
body: Dated but still heard, affectionate rather than harsh. (глупыш, дурачок)
examples: Don't be such a goose — of course they invited you.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
body: (в устойчивых выражениях)
examples: Her skin broke out in goose bumps. (also goosebumps; the modifier stays singular)
That was a wild goose chase — the address didn't even exist.
What's good for the goose is good for the gander.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the geese are flying south
entries.contrast: Mongoose is not related to this word — it came from Marathi centuries later — so its plural is mongooses, never ✗ mongeese. Likewise moose is unchanged in the plural: one moose, two moose.

entries.meaning: The small rodent; also the hand-held pointing device, which inherited the animal's irregular plural.
examples: A mouse ran across the kitchen floor.
We caught three mice in the garage last week.
The cat brought a dead mouse to the door.
My mouse stopped scrolling.
The lab replaced all the keyboards and mice.
She was quiet as a mouse all through dinner.

senses.head: The rodent
body: (мышь)
examples: A mouse ran across the kitchen floor.
We caught three mice in the garage last week.
The cat brought a dead mouse to the door.

senses.head: The computer device
body: Named for its resemblance to the animal, and it took the animal's plural with it. (компьютерная мышь)
examples: My mouse stopped scrolling.
The lab replaced all the keyboards and mice.

senses.head: A timid person
body: Usually in the fixed adjective mousy, or as a direct comparison. (тихоня, робкий человек)
examples: She was quiet as a mouse all through dinner.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the mice are in the attic
entries.variants: computer sense: mice is standard, mouses is occasionally used by manufacturers
entries.contrast: The noun ends in a voiceless /s/; the verb mouse and the plural of the unrelated verb sense can voice it. Compare house /haʊs/ (noun) with houses /ˈhaʊzɪz/ — the same voicing shift, though house is a regular plural.

entries.meaning: The parasitic insect — in practice almost always plural — and, informally, a contemptible person.
examples: The school sent a note home about head lice.
A single louse can lay several eggs a day.
The shelter treated the dogs for lice and fleas.
That louse never paid back a cent.
The two of them are absolute louses.
Don't louse up the interview by showing up late.

senses.head: The insect
body: Nearly always encountered as the plural lice, and most often in the compound head lice. (вошь)
examples: The school sent a note home about head lice.
A single louse can lay several eggs a day.
The shelter treated the dogs for lice and fleas.

senses.head: A contemptible person
body: Informal and dated, but instantly understood. This sense takes the regular plural. (подлец, мерзавец)
examples: That louse never paid back a cent.
The two of them are absolute louses.

senses.head: louse up — to ruin
body: Informal, always with up. (испортить, завалить)
examples: Don't louse up the interview by showing up late.

entries.agreement: plural verb — head lice are common in schools
entries.variants: in the 'contemptible person' sense the plural is regular — louses
entries.contrast: The two senses take different plurals. Insects are lice; people are louses. The related phrasal verb louse up means to ruin something.

entries.meaning: A small carnivorous mammal of Africa and Asia, famous for killing snakes. Listed here only because it is the trap that the goose → geese pattern sets.
examples: A mongoose killed the cobra in the courtyard.
Mongooses were introduced to the islands and devastated the birds.
The zoo's two mongooses share an enclosure.
He wrote a story about a mongoose named Rikki-Tikki-Tavi.
Unlike geese, mongooses take a perfectly regular plural.

senses.head: The animal
body: (мангуст)
examples: A mongoose killed the cobra in the courtyard.
Mongooses were introduced to the islands and devastated the birds.
The zoo's two mongooses share an enclosure.
He wrote a story about a mongoose named Rikki-Tikki-Tavi.
Unlike geese, mongooses take a perfectly regular plural.

entries.contrast: ✗ mongeese is the classic false analogy and is always wrong. The word has nothing to do with goose: it came into English from Marathi maṅgūs, long after i-mutation had stopped operating.
